body.objective: Students will be able to name days and daily activities.
body.iCan: I can name days and daily activities.
successCriteria: I can name the days of the week in Spanish
I can say what I do on different days

body.hook: Lunes, martes, miércoles… The Spanish days of the week come from the planets and gods of ancient Rome: lunes from the Moon (luna), martes from Mars. Today you'll learn them along with everyday activities.

study.title: Los días
study.question: How do I talk about days and activities in Spanish?
study.passage:
Days (written for this lesson): lunes, martes, miércoles, jueves, viernes, sábado, domingo. In Spanish, days are not capitalized, and the week usually starts on Monday.
Origins: lunes (luna, Moon), martes (Marte, Mars), miércoles (Mercurio, Mercury), jueves (Júpiter), viernes (Venus); sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from Latin for "Lord's day."
el lunes = on (this) Monday; los lunes = on Mondays (every week).
Activities: Los lunes, practico fútbol. Los miércoles, tengo clase de piano. El sábado, visito a mis abuelos. Los domingos, descanso.
Questions: ¿Qué día es hoy? Hoy es jueves. ¿Qué haces los sábados?
Activity: make a weekly planner in Spanish with one activity per day, then share with a partner who asks ¿Qué haces los martes?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to describe my routine.
successCriteria: I can describe my daily routine in Spanish
I can use common reflexive verbs in the yo form
I can use time and sequence words
body.hook: "Me levanto a las siete, desayuno, voy a la escuela…" Describing your daily routine is one of the most common conversations in any language class, and it uses some new verbs that point back at yourself.

study.title: Mi rutina diaria
study.question: How do I describe my daily routine in Spanish?
study.passage:
Text (read aloud, written for this lesson):
Los días de escuela, me despierto a las seis y media. Primero, me levanto y me ducho. Luego, me visto y desayuno cereal con fruta. A las ocho, voy a la escuela en autobús. Después de las clases, hago la tarea y practico hockey. Ceno con mi familia a las seis. Por la noche, leo un libro y me acuesto a las diez.
Reflexive verbs: the action is done to yourself, so they use me (myself): me levanto (I get myself up). For now, learn the yo forms as chunks.
Frequency words: siempre (always), a veces (sometimes), nunca (never), todos los días (every day).
Sequence: primero, luego, después, finalmente.
Activity: put picture cards of a routine in order and narrate them; then write your own routine and compare with a partner.
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
discussion: What time does the writer wake up?
Why do reflexive verbs use me?
Which part of your routine is the same as the writer's?
What do you do every day?
study.product: Write your weekday routine with at least eight activities, times, sequence words and two frequency words.

body.objective: Students will be able to compare routines across cultures.
body.iCan: I can compare routines across cultures.
successCriteria: I can describe routines in Spanish-speaking countries
I can compare them with my own routine
I can explain why routines differ across cultures
body.hook: In Spain, many families eat their main meal around 2 p.m. and dinner after 9 p.m. In Mexico, the big meal, la comida, also comes in the afternoon. How does your daily routine compare?

study.title: Rutinas del mundo
study.question: How do daily routines differ across cultures?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson; general patterns, and every family is different):
España: many people eat a light breakfast, a main meal (la comida) around 2–3 p.m. and dinner (la cena) around 9–10 p.m. School often runs until early or mid-afternoon. The traditional siesta (afternoon rest) is less common in big cities today but still exists, especially in summer.
México: the main meal, la comida, is often eaten in the mid-afternoon with family; dinner is usually lighter.
Argentina: dinner is often eaten late, after 9 p.m.
Canadá: many families eat lunch around noon and dinner around 6 p.m.
Comparison sentences: En España, cenan más tarde que en Canadá. En México, la comida es la comida principal. En cambio, en Canadá, la cena es la comida principal. Igual que en Canadá, los estudiantes en México van a la escuela por la mañana.
Activity: make a timeline comparing a school day in Canada with one in Spain or Mexico; write five comparison sentences and one reason why routines differ (climate, work hours, traditions).
study.source: Summary of general cultural patterns written for this lesson; routines vary by family and region.
